<div id="toc" class="toc"> <div id="toctitle">Table des matières</div> <ul class="sectlevel1"> <li><a href="#_the_problem_that_makes_everyone_flee">The Problem that Makes Everyone Flee</a></li> </ul> </div> <div id="preamble"> <div class="sectionbody"> <div class="paragraph"> <div class="title">reading time : 12 minutes</div> <p>I don&#8217;t hire an LLM. I hire an anonymizer. Before doing pgvector RAG, before fine-tuning CDA/FPA experts, before provisioning client workspaces — someone has to clean the data toilets. That employee is the anonymization expert (MVP0, EPIC 2 of codebase-gradle). And it&#8217;s him who makes the product marketable.</p> </div> <div class="dlist"> <dl> <dt class="hdlist1">toc</dt> <dd> <p>[no output]</p> </dd> </dl> </div> </div> </div> <div class="sect1"> <h2 id="_the_problem_that_makes_everyone_flee">The Problem that Makes Everyone Flee</h2> <div class="sectionbody"> <div class="paragraph"> <p>Every AI startup that manipulates training data runs into the same wall:</p> </div> <div class="listingblock"> <div class="content"> <pre class="highlightjs highlight"><code class="language-none hljs">---- ---- Données brutes client (SPG, cours, évaluations) ├→ Noms de stagiaires en clair dans les PDF ├→ Emails dans les métadonnées JSON ├→ IP de connexion dans les logs pgvector ├→ Identifiants dans les nœuds Graphify └→ Références OF pilote dans les schémas SQL ----
Result: either you do RAG on dirty data (PII hallucinations, GDPR non-compliance, legal risk), or you do nothing (no product). The third way — cleaning manually — is not scalable.
My answer: do not circumvent the problem. L'**automate**.
== MVP0: The Anonymizer, First Hired During the Probation Period
The MVP0 is not a feature. It's a**convenience expert**— an employee who does the dirty, mean, stupid work, and whom nobody wants to talk about in pitch decks.
What it does :
[source] ---- ENTRÉE : Données brutes multi-sources ├→ AsciiDoc (SPG_A2SP.adoc) → noms, dates, OF pilote ├→ JSON (catalogue formations) → emails, téléphones ├→ YAML (config workspace) → tokens OAuth2 ├→ SQL (schémas DDL) → IP, adresses ├→ pgvector (métadonnées embeddings) → identifiants ├→ ONNX (outputs classification) → noms propres └→ Graphify (graph.json) → nœuds avec PII
SORTIE : Datasets propres, format standardisé ├→ [ANONYMIZED] remplace les PII détectées ├→ Classification RGPD (niveau 0→4) ├→ Rapport d'audit (quoi a été nettoyé) └→ Dataset prêt pour RAG ET fine-tuning ----
It detects the most obvious patterns first (emails`.*@.*`, tokens`sk-*`, `ghp_*`, IPs), then it learns. The trial period is that: we validate that it does not let false negatives pass before making it permanent.
== What this MVP unlocks (and it's not just compliance)
Anonymization as MVP0 is not the GDPR toll before the highway. It's the highway itself. Here's what it opens:
=== Present : Augmented Reality in Prompt
[source] ---- DONNÉES BRUTES CLIENT ↓ Anonymiseur MVP0 → datasets propres ↓ RAG pgvector (MVP1) → top-K documents similaires (filtrés, anonymisés) ↓ LLM (deepseek-v4-pro) → réponse augmentée, zéro PII ----
RAG doesn’t search in dirty data — it searches in a space**clean by construction**. This changes everything for answer quality: the LLM doesn't spend its time trying to avoid PII it recognizes but must not mention.
=== Future : Fine-Tuning on Healthy Data
[source] ---- MVP0 → datasets propres accumulés (session après session) ↓ Fine-tuning expert métier (CDA, FPA) sur données zéro PII ↓ Modèle fine-tuné exposé via Ollama (sans fuite de données) ----
Fine-tuning on raw data is a potential legal disaster. On clean data, it's a**reproducible method**. Each client accumulates its cleaned datasets, each client can fine-tune its business experts on its data — never exposing personal data.
== Why It's Marketable
It is not « a GDPR compliance tool ». It is a**reproducible method that transforms a universal problem into an asset** :
1. *Every training company has dirty data* — that's the problem 2. *There is no automated multi-source cleaning pipeline* — that's the market 3. *The loop: anonymization → RAG → fine-tuning is proprietary* — that's the barrier
Edster SaaS (MVP3) will not sell 'a Gradle workspace'. It will sell this closed loop. And MVP0 is the entry point.
== The SQL Format as the Third Way of Context
Importing structured data is not just an exchange format. The SQL schema (DDL) carries the**entity-relationship model of the domain** :
[source] ---- CREATE TABLE formation ( id UUID PRIMARY KEY, titre VARCHAR NOT NULL, referentiel RNCP REFERENCES rncp(id), organisme OF REFERENCES of_pilote(id) -- ← va être anonymisé ); ----
This DDL, once anonymized (line 4), becomes a source of context for the LLM. Not text — of**business model**. The RAG gives the content (vector similarity), Graphify gives the relationships (exact structure), and the SQL schema gives the**implicit Domain-Driven Design**bounded contexts, aggregates, value objects. The LLM understands the business because it reads its schema.
== The Roadmap: from MVP0 to SaaS
[source] ---- MVP0 — Anonymiseur (ce que cet article décrit) Sortie : datasets propres, reproductible
MVP1 — RAG pgvector (dépend de MVP0) Realité augmentée en prompt sur données nettoyées
MVP2 — Graphify + ONNX + SQL DDD (dépend de MVP1) Vecteur composite de contexte (règles + similarité + relations exactes)
MVP3 — SaaS Edster (dépend de MVP0-2) Provisionnement workspace client complet ----
Each MVP depends on the previous one. None can be delivered without MVP0. That's why the Anonymizer is not 'P0' in the backlog — it is**MVP0**. This is the first commercial deliverable, and everything else depends on its success.
== Conclusion: The Invisible Work That Makes Everything Possible
In a traditional startup, data cleaning is outsourced, manual, or ignored. In this architecture, it's the**heart of the product**. The Anonymiser is the first employee because without him, nothing works :
* Without MVP0 → no legal RAG (MVP1) * Without MVP0 → no fine-tuning without data leak (EPIC 5) * Without MVP0 → no credible SaaS (MVP3) * Without MVP0 → no augmented reality in prompt * Without MVP0 → no third context path (SQL DDD)
He does the dirty work. He will never be mentioned in the pitches. But he's the one who keeps the factory running.
And that's why we hire them first.
== References
* Article on spatial ontology and trust circles :link:../2026/0114_gouvernance_cercles_confiance_ontologie_spatiale_alignement_llm_post.html[The Spatial Ontology as Alignment Mechanism] * Article on Eager/Lazy agent governance:link:../2026/0108_gouvernance_agent_opencode_eager_lazy_post.html[Governing an AI Agent with AsciiDoc] * Article on the Hot/Warm/Cold mechanism:link:../2026/0110_mecanisme_backup_contexte_agent_post.html[Sliding Window and Cold Wave] * Article on the comparison of the three LLMs :link:../2026/0112_comparaison_kimi_glm_deepseek_long_contexte_plugin_gradle_opencode_post.html[DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K2.6, GLM-5.1] ----</code></pre> </div> </div> </div> </div>

<div id="toc" class="toc"> <div id="toctitle">Sommaire</div> <ul class="sectlevel1"> <li><a href="#_introduction">Introduction</a></li> <li><a href="#_pipeline_architecture">Pipeline Architecture</a></li> <li><a href="#_configuration_of_the_continuous_integration_ci_pipeline">Configuration of the Continuous Integration (CI) Pipeline</a> <ul class="sectlevel2"> <li><a href="#_ci_workflow_structure">CI Workflow Structure</a></li> <li><a href="#_analysis_of_ci_steps">Analysis of CI Steps</a> <ul class="sectlevel3"> <li><a href="#_triggers_on">Triggers (<code>on</code>)</a></li> </ul> </li> </ul> </li> </ul> </div> <div class="sect1"> <h2 id="_introduction">Introduction</h2> <div class="sectionbody"> <div class="paragraph"> <div class="title">Objectif : Accompany the reader in setting up a minimal but functional CI/CD pipeline for a Python application, with automatic deployment to PyPI.</div> <p>Automation of development processes has become indispensable in modern projects. A well-designed CI/CD pipeline enables not only early detection of regressions in the development cycle but also full automation of the deployment process.</p> </div> <div class="paragraph"> <p>In this article, we will explore how to set up a complete pipeline with GitHub Actions for a Python application, from continuous integration (CI) to continuous deployment (CD) on PyPI.</p> </div> </div> </div> <div class="sect1"> <h2 id="_pipeline_architecture">Pipeline Architecture</h2> <div class="sectionbody"> <div class="paragraph"> <p>Our pipeline consists of two distinct workflows:</p> </div> <div class="olist arabic"> <ol class="arabic"> <li> <p><strong>CI Pipeline</strong>Executed on every push and pull request</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>CD Pipeline</strong>: Triggered only on GitHub releases</p> </li> </ol> </div> <div class="imageblock"> <div class="content"> <img src="images/ci-cd-overview.svg" alt="ci cd overview" width="394" height="648"> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="sect1"> <h2 id="_configuration_of_the_continuous_integration_ci_pipeline">Configuration of the Continuous Integration (CI) Pipeline</h2> <div class="sectionbody"> <div class="sect2"> <h3 id="_ci_workflow_structure">CI Workflow Structure</h3> <div class="paragraph"> <p>The CI workflow is designed to validate every contribution to the code. Here is its full configuration:</p> </div> <div class="listingblock"> <div class="content"> <pre class="pygments highlight"><code data-lang="yaml">name: CI/CD Pipeline
on: push: branches: - main pull_request: branches: - main
jobs: build: runs-on: ubuntu-latest
steps: - name: Checkout code uses: actions/checkout@v4
- name: Set up Python uses: actions/setup-python@v5 with: python-version: '3.x'
- name: Install dependencies run: | python -m pip install --upgrade pip pip install -r requirements.txt pip install ruff pytest pytest-mock
- name: Run Linting (Ruff) run: ruff check .
- name: Run Tests (Pytest) run: pytest</code></pre> </div> </div> </div> <div class="sect2"> <h3 id="_analysis_of_ci_steps">Analysis of CI Steps</h3> <div class="sect3"> <h4 id="_triggers_on">Triggers (<code>on</code>)</h4> <div class="listingblock"> <div class="content"> <pre class="pygments highlight"><code data-lang="yaml">---- ---- on: push: branches: - main pull_request: branches: - main ----
The pipeline triggers on: - Each push to the branch`main` - Each pull request towards`main`
This approach ensures that the main code remains stable and that any contribution is validated before integration.
==== 2. Execution Environment
----
runs-on: ubuntu-latest
Ubuntu Latest offers a good compromise between performance, cost, and compatibility for most Python projects.
==== 3. Checkout of the Code
```yaml ---- ---- - name: Checkout code uses: actions/checkout@v4 ----
The action`checkout@v4`Retrieves the source code from the repository. Version v4 brings performance and security improvements.
==== 4. Python Configuration
----
- name: Set up Python uses: actions/setup-python@v5 with: python-version: '3.x'
The use of`'3.x'`allows automatically using the latest stable version of Python 3, simplifying maintenance.
==== 5. Installation of Dependencies
```yaml ---- ---- - name: Install dependencies run: | python -m pip install --upgrade pip pip install -r requirements.txt pip install ruff pytest pytest-mock ----
This step: - Update pip to the latest version - Install the project dependencies - Add the development tools (linting and tests)
==== 6. Linting with Ruff
----
- name: Run Linting (Ruff) run: ruff check .
**Ruff**is an ultra-fast Python linter written in Rust. It combines the features of several tools (Flake8, Black, isort) into a single high-performance tool.
==== 7. Execution of Tests
```yaml ---- ---- - name: Run Tests (Pytest) run: pytest ----
Pytest runs the entire test suite, ensuring that changes do not introduce regressions.
== Configuration of the Deployment Pipeline (CD)
=== CD Workflow Structure
The CD workflow triggers only on GitHub releases and automates publishing to PyPI:
[source,yaml] ---- name: Publish to PyPI
on: release: types: - published
jobs: deploy: runs-on: ubuntu-latest
steps: - name: Checkout code uses: actions/checkout@v4
- name: Set up Python uses: actions/setup-python@v5 with: python-version: '3.x'
- name: Install dependencies run: | python -m pip install --upgrade pip pip install setuptools wheel twine
- name: Build and publish env: TWINE_USERNAME: __token__ TWINE_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.PYPI_API_TOKEN }} run: | python setup.py sdist bdist_wheel twine upload dist/* ----
=== Analysis of CD Steps
==== 1. Trigger Release
----
on: release: types: - published
The CD pipeline is triggered only when a GitHub release is published. This approach ensures precise control over deployments.
==== 2. Installation of Build Tools
```yaml ---- ---- pip install setuptools wheel twine ----
- **setuptools**: Python packaging tools - **wheel**: Modern Python distribution format - **twine**: Secure tool for uploading to PyPI
==== 3. Configuration of Authentication
----
env: TWINE_USERNAME: __token__ TWINE_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.PYPI_API_TOKEN }}
Authentication uses a PyPI API token stored as a GitHub secret, which is more secure than classic credentials.
==== 4. Build and Publication
```yaml ---- ---- run: | python setup.py sdist bdist_wheel twine upload dist/* ----
- `sdist`Create a source distribution - `bdist_wheel`: Create a wheel (binary distribution) - `twine upload`: Publish the distributions on PyPI
== Python Package Configuration
=== Structure of setup.py
For the pipeline to work, your project must include a file`setup.py`:
[source,python] ---- from setuptools import setup, find_packages
with open("README.adoc", "r", encoding="utf-8") as fh: long_description = fh.read()
setup( name="playlist-downloader", version="1.0.0", author="Votre Nom", author_email="votre.email@example.com", description="CLI tool for managing YouTube playlists", long_description=long_description, long_description_content_type="text/plain", url="https://github.com/cheroliv/playlist-downloader", packages=find_packages(), classifiers=[ "Development Status :: 4 - Beta", "Intended Audience :: Developers", "License :: OSI Approved :: MIT License", "Operating System :: OS Independent", "Programming Language :: Python :: 3", "Programming Language :: Python :: 3.8", "Programming Language :: Python :: 3.9", "Programming Language :: Python :: 3.10", "Programming Language :: Python :: 3.11", ], python_requires="&gt;=3.8", install_requires=[ "typer&gt;=0.9.0", "yt-dlp&gt;=2023.1.6", "google-api-python-client&gt;=2.70.0", "google-auth-oauthlib&gt;=0.7.1", "pymonad&gt;=2.4.0", "pyyaml&gt;=6.0", ], entry_points={ "console_scripts": [ "playlist-downloader=cli:app", ], }, ) ----
=== Key Points of setup.py
1. **Metadata**: Name, version, author, description 2. **Dependencies**: List of required packages 3. **Entry Points**: Exposed CLI commands 4. **Classifiers**: Metadata for PyPI
== Securing with GitHub Secrets
=== PyPI Token Configuration
1. **Create an API token on PyPI**(empty)
- Log in to PyPI - Go to Account Settings &gt; API tokens - Create a new token with appropriate permissions
1. **Add the secret in GitHub**(empty)
- Repository Settings &gt; Secrets and variables &gt; Actions - Create a new secret named`PYPI_API_TOKEN` - Paste your token PyPI
[plantuml, secrets-flow, svg] ---- @startuml !theme plain
actor Developer as dev participant "GitHub Repository" as repo participant "GitHub Actions" as actions participant PyPI
dev -&gt; repo : Configure PYPI_API_TOKEN secret repo -&gt; actions : Trigger CD pipeline on release actions -&gt; actions : Access secret securely actions -&gt; PyPI : Authenticate with token PyPI -&gt; PyPI : Validate and publish package
note over actions, PyPI Token never exposed in logs Automatic rotation possible end note
@enduml ----
== Full Deployment Workflow
=== Deployment Sequence
[plantuml, deployment-sequence, svg] ---- @startuml !theme plain
actor Developer as dev participant "Local Git" as git participant "GitHub" as github participant "GitHub Actions" as actions participant PyPI participant "End Users" as users
dev -&gt; git : git tag v1.0.0 dev -&gt; git : git push origin v1.0.0 git -&gt; github : Push tag dev -&gt; github : Create release from tag github -&gt; actions : Trigger CD pipeline actions -&gt; actions : Checkout code actions -&gt; actions : Setup Python environment actions -&gt; actions : Install build tools actions -&gt; actions : Build distributions (sdist + wheel) actions -&gt; PyPI : Upload to PyPI with token PyPI -&gt; PyPI : Validate and publish users -&gt; PyPI : pip install playlist-downloader
note over dev, github Release creation can be automated or done manually through GitHub UI end note
@enduml ----
=== Pipeline States
[plantuml, pipeline-states, svg] ---- @startuml !theme plain
[*] --&gt; Idle
Idle --&gt; CI_Running : Push/PR created CI_Running --&gt; CI_Success : All checks pass CI_Running --&gt; CI_Failed : Linting/Tests fail CI_Success --&gt; Idle : Merge completed CI_Failed --&gt; Idle : Fix and retry
Idle --&gt; CD_Running : Release published CD_Running --&gt; CD_Success : Package published CD_Running --&gt; CD_Failed : Build/Upload error CD_Success --&gt; Idle : Package available on PyPI CD_Failed --&gt; Idle : Fix and retry release
note on link #red : Blocks merge note on link #green : Allows deployment
@enduml ----
== Best Practices and Optimizations
=== 1. Version Management
Use semantic Git tags:
----
git tag -a v1.2.3 -m "Release version 1.2.3" git push origin v1.2.3
=== 2. Matrix Tests
To test on multiple Python versions:
```yaml ---- ---- strategy: matrix: python-version: [3.8, 3.9, "3.10", "3.11"] ----
=== 3. Dependencies cache
Speed up builds with the cache:
----
- name: Cache pip dependencies uses: actions/cache@v3 with: path: ~/.cache/pip key: ${{ runner.os }}-pip-${{ hashFiles('**/requirements.txt') }}
=== 4. Deployment Environments
Use GitHub environments for controlled deployments:
```yaml ---- ---- jobs: deploy: environment: production runs-on: ubuntu-latest ----
== Use Cases and Architecture
=== Use Case Diagram
[plantuml, use-cases, svg] ---- @startuml !theme plain
left to right direction
actor "Developer" as dev actor "GitHub Actions" as ga actor "End User" as user
package "CI/CD System" { usecase "Run Linting" as lint usecase "Execute Tests" as test usecase "Build Package" as build usecase "Publish to PyPI" as publish usecase "Create Release" as release }
dev --&gt; lint : Pushes code dev --&gt; test : Pushes code dev --&gt; release : Creates release ga --&gt; build : On release trigger ga --&gt; publish : After successful build user --&gt; publish : Downloads package
lint .&gt; test : triggers test .&gt; build : on success build .&gt; publish : on success
@enduml ----
=== Deployment Architecture
[plantuml, deployment-architecture, svg] ---- @startuml !theme plain
cloud "GitHub" { [Source Repository] [GitHub Actions] [Secrets Store] }
cloud "PyPI" { [Package Registry] [Distribution Files] }
node "CI/CD Pipeline" { [Linting] [Testing] [Building] [Publishing] }
[Source Repository] --&gt; [GitHub Actions] : Triggers [GitHub Actions] --&gt; [Linting] [Linting] --&gt; [Testing] [Testing] --&gt; [Building] [Building] --&gt; [Publishing] [Publishing] --&gt; [Package Registry] : Uploads [Secrets Store] --&gt; [Publishing] : Provides token
note as N1 Secure token-based authentication end note
[Secrets Store] .. N1
@enduml ----
== Monitoring and Debugging
=== Logs and Monitoring
GitHub Actions provides detailed logs for each step. To debug:
1. **Examine the logs**of each step 2. **Enable debug**with`ACTIONS_STEP_DEBUG` 3. **Use some artifacts**to save the build files
----
- name: Upload build artifacts uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3 if: failure() with: name: build-logs path: build/
=== Notifications
Add Slack or email notifications:
```yaml ---- ---- - name: Notify on failure if: failure() uses: 8398a7/action-slack@v3 with: status: ${{ job.status }} webhook_url: ${{ secrets.SLACK_WEBHOOK }} ----
== Conclusion
Setting up a robust CI/CD pipeline with GitHub Actions radically transforms the development experience. By automating linting, tests, and deployment, you:
- **Reduce the errors**in production - **Accelerate the cycles**of development - **Improve the trust**in your releases - **Facilitate collaboration**as a team
This pipeline can be adapted to different types of Python projects by adjusting linting tools, testing frameworks, or deployment targets.
The initial investment in configuring these workflows is quickly recouped through time savings and the reduction of manual errors during deployments.
== Additional Resources
- https://docs.github.com/en/actions[Documentation GitHub Actions] - https://packaging.python.org/[Python Packaging Guide] - https://docs.pytest.org/[Documentation Pytest] - https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/[Documentation Ruff] - https://twine.readthedocs.io/[Twine documentation]
✅ Functional pipeline reached ! You now have a simple CI/CD pipeline that lets you automate your tests and publish your Python package to PyPI directly from GitHub Actions.
However, this pipeline remains deliberately minimalist. It does not yet cover some essential aspects in a professional context:
Multi-version tests of Python,
Automatic security analysis,
Gradual deployment via Test PyPI,
Pipeline monitoring and metrics,
Automation of versioning and integration of modern best practices (pyproject.toml).
In the next part, we will move to the next level. You will learn to transform this basic pipeline into a true industrial deployment chain, robust and secure, ready for production Python projects. ----</code></pre> </div> </div> </div> </div> </div> </div>

item.description:
<div class="paragraph"> <p>Here is a working piece of Groovy code,<br> to change all occurrences of a character sequence in a String<br> and load a .properties file into a Properties object.<br> Execute a command in a String.<br> replaceTextinFile.groovy<br></p> </div> <div class="listingblock"> <div class="content"> <pre class="highlight"><code class="language-groovy" data-lang="groovy">#!/usr/bin/env groovy println System.getProperty("user.home")
static String getSeparator_() { System.getProperty("file.separator") }
String separator = separator_
String path = System.getProperty("user.home") .concat("${separator}.gradle" + separator + "gradle.properties")
File propertiesFile = new File(path)
assert propertiesFile.exists() &amp;&amp; !propertiesFile.directory
Properties gradleProperties = new Properties()
propertiesFile.withInputStream { InputStream it -&gt; gradleProperties.load(it) }
String user_name = gradleProperties.getProperty("user_name")
String text String resultText text = new File("${System.getProperty("user.home")}" + separator + "src" + separator + "cheroliv.github.io" + separator + "src" + separator + "main" + separator + "resources" + separator + "eco_space.txt").text
String to = separator + "media" + separator + "${user_name}" + separator + "320" + separator + "videoCours" + separator String from = "${System.getProperty("user.home")}" + separator + "p2p" + separator
resultText = text.replace(to, from)
println resultText
//execute command line in a string println "rsync -avr ${resultText} ${to}".execute().text</code></pre> </div> </div>
